Right. I am Sanjay. Shall we start with the numbers? Study A is much bigger.
Dejair. Yes, four hundred against sixty. But the follow-up in B is much longer.
Two years against six months. That is a big difference for pain.
And study B measured pain at home. That is more difficult, but it is closer to real life.
True. Their method is also clearer. Step by step, not one paragraph.
So which one do we choose? We have two minutes.
A, I think. It is the bigger study, and bigger is safer.
I do not agree, and this is why. My patients live far from the hospital, like theirs. For me B is more relevant, even if it is smaller.
That is a good point. So we say A is the better study and B is the more useful one for us.
Exactly. And that is a clearer answer than choosing only one.

Good afternoon and welcome to the workshop. My name is Olga and I am facilitating this session. Before we start, three things about how this works. This is not a lecture. You are going to work in pairs, and every pair gets two studies to compare. Second, keep your answers brief. You have two minutes each, and the most common problem in this room is not silence, it is people who talk for eight minutes. Third, and this is the important one. I do not want you to tell me which study is better. I want you to tell me why. Better is easy. Why is the difficult part, and why is the reason we are here.

So, my pair and I looked at the two studies. The first one is much bigger, about four hundred patients, and the second one has only sixty. But bigger is not the same as more useful. The small study is far more detailed. They followed each patient for two years, they measured pain at home, not in the hospital, and their method is clearer than anything in the large study. For my own work, the smaller one is more relevant, because my patients also live far from the hospital. If somebody asks me which is the better study, I would say the large one. If somebody asks me which one I am going to use, it is the small one.
